title: How to Steal CPU Idle Time When Synchronous I/O Mode Becomes Promising
problem: Synchronous I/O with ultra-low-latency storage causes substantial busy waiting and CPU underutilization during I/O operations. The narrowed performance gap between storage and CPU makes synchronous I/O viable but introduces idle cycles.
motivation: Ultra-low-latency storage devices are enabling synchronous I/O adoption, but current approaches waste CPU cycles and reduce overall system utilization.
method: The Idle-Time-Stealing (ITS) design uses three coordinated threads: a self-improving thread performing prefetching for high-priority processes during synchronous I/O idle periods, an I/O-waiting process continuing instruction execution when justified, and a self-sacrificing thread proactively switching low-priority I/O from synchronous to asynchronous mode.
key_novelty: Dynamically harvesting CPU idle cycles from synchronous I/O waits for prefetching and execution of higher-priority work while adaptively rebalancing I/O modes by priority.
contributions: Idle-Time-Stealing (ITS) architecture for CPU idle time reduction in synchronous I/O scenarios
Self-improving prefetching thread that exploits idle periods for high-priority processes
Priority-aware adaptive switching of low-priority I/O between synchronous and asynchronous modes
Thread-level coordination mechanism reducing CPU idle time in modern low-latency storage systems
primary_theme: CPU idle time exploitation during synchronous I/O
